title: Bio-inorganic Chemistry

toc.title: 15.1 Micro- and macronutrients and the biological roles of metal ions
15.2 The sodium–potassium pump and sodium–glucose cotransport
15.3 Toxicity of iron, arsenic, mercury, lead and cadmium

html:
This short chapter carries about 2 questions, but it joins the periodic table directly to physiology and medicine.

The same principles used throughout inorganic chemistry — oxidation state, ligand binding, ionic size, solubility and redox reactivity — decide why a metal ion can be an enzyme cofactor at one dose and a poison at another.

Learn each element through four hooks: where it is concentrated, what molecule or enzyme uses it, what breaks in deficiency, and what breaks in excess. That pattern will also serve you in Zoology, physiology and pharmacology.

What the paper asks from this chapter
  • Macrominerals are needed in relatively large daily amounts. Among the elements in this chapter: Na, K, Mg and Ca. Microminerals/trace elements here are Zn, Cu, Co, Ni, Fe and Cr.
  • Na⁺ is the dominant extracellular cation; K⁺ is the dominant intracellular cation. Their gradients control fluid volume, membrane potential and excitability.
  • Mg²⁺ is the central ion of chlorophyll and the usual partner of ATP in cells (MgATP). Ca²⁺ builds bone mineral and also acts in clotting, muscle contraction, secretion and signalling.
  • Zn²⁺ is a redox-inert Lewis acid in carbonic anhydrase, carboxypeptidase and zinc-finger proteins. Cu and Fe are useful because they change oxidation state readily; the same redox activity makes free Fe/Cu dangerous.
  • Cobalt is biologically useful to humans as the centre of vitamin B₁₂ (cobalamin); inorganic cobalt in food cannot be converted by human cells into B₁₂.
  • Nickel is a true cofactor in plant and microbial enzymes such as urease, but a specific essential biochemical function in humans is not yet established. Cr(III) was traditionally linked with insulin action, but modern reviews also find human essentiality unproved; Cr(VI), by contrast, is highly toxic and carcinogenic.
  • The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase uses one ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in. It is primary active transport and is inhibited by ouabain and cardiac glycosides such as digoxin.
  • A sodium–glucose transporter (SGLT) is not an ATP-burning pump. It is a secondary-active Na⁺ symporter: intestinal/renal SGLT1 generally couples 2 Na⁺ to 1 glucose, whereas early proximal-tubule SGLT2 couples 1 Na⁺ to 1 glucose. Oral rehydration solution exploits intestinal SGLT1.
  • Toxic metals often work by ionic mimicry and thiol binding: arsenate imitates phosphate; As(III), Hg and Pb bind –SH groups; Pb²⁺ imitates Ca²⁺/Zn²⁺; Cd²⁺ imitates Zn²⁺/Ca²⁺.
  • Disease hooks: iron overload → liver, heart and endocrine damage by hydroxyl-radical chemistry; arsenic → skin changes, neuropathy and cancers; methylmercury → Minamata-type brain injury; lead → impaired neurodevelopment and haem synthesis; cadmium → renal tubular injury and painful bone disease (Itai-itai).

15.1 Micro- and macronutrients and the biological roles of metal ions

An essential element is not merely an element found in tissue. Strictly, removing it should reproducibly impair a biological function, restoring it should repair that function, and ideally a direct biochemical role should be known.

This strict definition is why the status of chromium and nickel in human nutrition remains more cautious than in many older textbooks.

Mineral nutrients are often divided by the amount required. Macrominerals are needed at roughly hundreds of milligrams or more per day; microminerals are needed in milligram or microgram amounts.

The division says nothing about importance: a trace of cobalt inside vitamin B₁₂ is indispensable for blood formation, while a tiny excess of potassium in plasma can stop the heart.

Biology also cares about speciation — the exact chemical form. Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ differ in transport, Cr(III) and Cr(VI) differ dramatically in hazard, and methylmercury crosses membranes far more effectively than inorganic mercury salts.

Metal ions perform four recurring chemical jobs. First, they provide charge and osmotic balance (Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺). Second, they act as Lewis acids that polarize bonds in enzyme active sites, especially Zn²⁺ and Mg²⁺.

Third, Fe and Cu perform electron transfer and oxygen chemistry because neighbouring oxidation states are accessible.

Fourth, ions can be structural or signalling agents: Ca²⁺ in bone and cytosolic signals, Zn²⁺ in zinc-finger domains that hold transcription factors in the correct shape for DNA binding.

Element Chemical/biological role Deficiency or imbalance hook
Sodium (Na⁺) Main extracellular cation; sets effective plasma osmolality and extracellular-fluid volume; Na⁺ influx produces the upstroke of many action potentials; its gradient drives nutrient and ion cotransport Losses with vomiting, diarrhoea or diuretics cause volume depletion; abnormal plasma Na⁺ mainly signals water imbalance and can produce confusion, seizures or coma
Potassium (K⁺) Main intracellular cation; K⁺ leak through membrane channels is the main immediate reason the resting membrane is negative inside; needed for nerve conduction, muscle contraction and several enzymes, including pyruvate kinase Hypokalaemia causes weakness and cardiac arrhythmias; hyperkalaemia is an emergency because cardiac excitability and conduction fail
Magnesium (Mg²⁺) Cofactor in hundreds of reactions; most intracellular ATP is present as MgATP; stabilizes DNA, RNA and ribosomes; required by kinases and by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase; central atom of chlorophyll in plants Deficiency gives tremor, cramps, arrhythmias and resistant K⁺/Ca²⁺ abnormalities; most body Mg is in bone and cells, so a normal plasma value can hide depletion
Calcium (Ca²⁺) About 99% is in bone and teeth as hydroxyapatite, Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂; ionized Ca²⁺ is clotting factor IV, triggers neurotransmitter and hormone release, enables troponin-mediated muscle contraction and binds calmodulin in signalling Childhood deficiency contributes to rickets; adult bone loss gives osteomalacia/osteoporosis; acute hypocalcaemia increases excitability and can cause tetany
Zinc (Zn²⁺) Catalytic and structural ion in carbonic anhydrase, carboxypeptidase, alcohol dehydrogenase, Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase, polymerases and zinc-finger transcription factors; important in growth, immunity, taste and wound repair Poor growth, delayed sexual maturation, hair loss, skin lesions, impaired taste and poor wound healing; chronic excess induces copper deficiency
Copper (Cu⁺/Cu²⁺) Redox centre in cytochrome-c oxidase, Cu/Zn superoxide dismutase, lysyl oxidase for collagen/elastin cross-linking, dopamine β-hydroxylase and tyrosinase; ceruloplasmin carries Cu and oxidizes Fe²⁺ for iron transport Deficiency can cause anaemia, neutropenia, poor pigmentation and connective-tissue weakness; Menkes disease impairs Cu transport, while Wilson disease causes Cu accumulation in liver and brain
Cobalt (Co) Central ion of cobalamin (vitamin B₁₂). B₁₂ is required by methionine synthase and methylmalonyl-CoA mutase, linking folate metabolism, DNA synthesis and myelin maintenance B₁₂ deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia and potentially irreversible neurological injury. Humans need preformed B₁₂ made by microorganisms; eating cobalt salts does not solve B₁₂ deficiency
Nickel (Ni) Established cofactor in microbial/plant urease and several hydrogenases; occurs in human tissues and may influence iron handling, but no definite human Ni-dependent enzyme is known No recognized human nickel-deficiency syndrome. Contact allergy is common; inhaled nickel compounds in industry are respiratory carcinogens
Iron (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺) In haemoglobin, myoglobin, cytochromes and catalase; in iron–sulfur clusters of respiratory-chain proteins; and in ribonucleotide reductase for DNA synthesis. Transferrin transports Fe³⁺ and ferritin stores it safely Iron-deficiency anaemia is microcytic and hypochromic; overload injures liver, heart, pancreas and other endocrine organs (§15.3)
Chromium (Cr) Traditional texts describe Cr(III) as part of a “glucose tolerance factor” and as an aid to insulin action. No human Cr-dependent enzyme has been firmly established, and major modern reviews regard essentiality as unproved No clearly defined Cr(III)-deficiency disease in people eating ordinary diets. Cr(VI) compounds are strong oxidants, enter cells through anion pathways and are established lung carcinogens

The iron and copper rows reveal the chapter's central chemical bargain. A redox-active metal is an excellent catalyst, but the cell must never leave much of it “free”.

Iron is therefore handed between proteins and locked in ferritin; copper is escorted by chaperones.

Zinc can occupy delicate structural sites more safely because Zn²⁺ has a filled 3d¹⁰ subshell and does not cycle between oxidation states under biological conditions.

Absorption is controlled most tightly for iron because humans have no regulated pathway for excreting a large iron excess.

In the duodenum, Fe³⁺ is reduced to Fe²⁺ for uptake; iron then leaves intestinal and storage cells through ferroportin. The liver hormone hepcidin blocks ferroportin when iron is plentiful or infection is present.

This is elegant bio-inorganic control: the body regulates the gate, not the drain.

“Present in the body” does not prove “essential”

Nickel and chromium illustrate why examination answers should follow established biochemical roles rather than supplement advertisements.

Nickel unquestionably serves in plant and microbial urease, and chromium(III) has been linked experimentally with carbohydrate metabolism, but neither has a firmly demonstrated, specific essential function in humans.

That caution does not make their toxic forms safe: nickel allergy and carcinogenic chromium(VI) are real occupational hazards.

The pump's hourly bill

Problem. A resting nerve cell hydrolyses 1.0 × 10⁹ ATP molecules per minute on its Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase alone. How many sodium ions leave and potassium ions enter per minute, and what net charge crosses outward?

Solution. Per ATP: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in.

Sodium out = 3 × 10⁹ per minute; potassium in = 2 × 10⁹ per minute; net outward charge = (3 − 2) × 10⁹ = 1.0 × 10⁹ positive charges per minute — the electrogenic leak the resting potential leans on.

One protein, three-to-two bookkeeping, a billion times a minute: bio-inorganic arithmetic in miniature.

15.2 The sodium–potassium pump and sodium–glucose cotransport

Almost every animal cell keeps Na⁺ high outside and K⁺ high inside. Typical plasma Na⁺ is near 145 mmol L⁻¹ while cytosolic Na⁺ is only about 10–15 mmol L⁻¹; cytosolic K⁺ is about 140 mmol L⁻¹ while plasma K⁺ is near 4–5 mmol L⁻¹.

These gradients are batteries. They store energy that powers electrical signalling, cell-volume control, pH regulation, Ca²⁺ handling and the uptake of glucose and amino acids.

The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase: primary active transport

The sodium–potassium pump is a P-type ATPase embedded in the plasma membrane. In each cycle it exports three Na⁺ ions, imports two K⁺ ions and hydrolyses one ATP. The cycle can be remembered as a two-door airlock:

  1. With the transporter open to the cytosol, 3 Na⁺ bind.
  2. ATP phosphorylates the pump; its shape changes and Na⁺ is released outside.
  3. In the outward-facing form, 2 K⁺ bind.
  4. Loss of phosphate returns the pump to the inward-facing shape, releasing K⁺ into the cytosol.

Because three positive charges leave for every two that enter, the pump is slightly electrogenic: it contributes a few millivolts to the negative interior.

Its larger role is indirect — it maintains the K⁺ gradient, and K⁺ leaking out through resting K⁺ channels makes the inside much more negative.

The pump also keeps cells from swelling: impermeant proteins inside the cell attract ions and water, but continuous Na⁺ export balances that osmotic pull.

Ouabain and the cardiac glycosides digoxin/digitoxin inhibit Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase from the extracellular side. In heart muscle, partial inhibition raises cytosolic Na⁺ slightly.

The Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger then expels less Ca²⁺, so more Ca²⁺ is available for contraction. Too much inhibition disturbs rhythm — a narrow boundary between drug and poison.

Hypokalaemia increases digoxin toxicity because K⁺ normally competes at the pump's extracellular side.

Sodium–glucose cotransport: secondary active transport

A sodium–glucose cotransporter (SGLT) uses the downhill entry of Na⁺ to drag glucose uphill into a cell. It does not hydrolyse ATP itself. The energy bill is paid afterwards by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, which pumps the entering Na⁺ back out.

Thus SGLT is secondary active transport, whereas the Na⁺/K⁺ pump is primary active transport.

Feature SGLT1 SGLT2
Main sites Small-intestinal brush border; later proximal renal tubule (S3) Early proximal renal tubule (S1/S2)
Coupling 2 Na⁺ : 1 glucose 1 Na⁺ : 1 glucose
Character High affinity, lower capacity; also transports galactose Lower affinity, high capacity; responsible for most renal glucose reabsorption
Clinical hook Basis of glucose-containing oral rehydration solution; genetic loss causes glucose–galactose malabsorption Blocked by gliflozin drugs, increasing urinary glucose excretion in type 2 diabetes

After glucose enters an intestinal or renal epithelial cell through apical SGLT, it leaves across the basolateral membrane mainly through a facilitative GLUT transporter. Water follows the absorbed solute osmotically.

This explains a life-saving treatment developed from pure transport chemistry: in cholera and other secretory diarrhoeas, the intestine secretes profusely, but SGLT1 remains functional.

A correctly balanced solution containing glucose and sodium therefore pulls Na⁺ and water back into the body. Plain glucose without salts, or a very sugary drink, does not reproduce that effect and may worsen osmotic loss.

Worked example 15.1 — who pays the ATP bill?

Problem. An intestinal cell takes up 300 glucose molecules through SGLT1. Assuming every co-transported Na⁺ is subsequently exported by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase, how many ATP molecules are used by the pump, and how many K⁺ ions enter during those pump cycles?

Solution. SGLT1 couples 2 Na⁺ to each glucose, so Na⁺ entry is 300 × 2 = 600 Na⁺. One pump cycle exports 3 Na⁺, requiring 600 ÷ 3 = 200 cycles and therefore 200 ATP. Each cycle imports 2 K⁺, so K⁺ entry is 200 × 2 = 400 K⁺.

SGLT itself uses no ATP; Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pays to restore the gradient.

A two-line memory lock

“3–2–1 pump; 2–1 gut.” The pump moves 3 Na⁺ and 2 K⁺ per 1 ATP; intestinal SGLT1 moves 2 Na⁺ with 1 glucose. Renal SGLT2 is the exception to complete: 1 Na⁺ with 1 glucose.

15.3 Toxicity of iron, arsenic, mercury, lead and cadmium

Toxicity is governed by dose, chemical form, route, age and nutritional state. A useful mechanistic map has four roads to injury. Ionic mimicry lets a toxic ion use another ion's transporter or binding site.

Thiol binding disables enzymes whose cysteine –SH groups are chemically vital. Redox cycling generates reactive oxygen species.

Finally, storage and biomagnification make exposure last: lead and cadmium are warehoused in the body, while methylmercury becomes more concentrated at higher levels of an aquatic food chain.

Chelation therapy follows the same coordination chemistry. A multidentate ligand wraps a metal ion and forms a more excretable complex.

It is never a general “detox”: the ligand may also remove essential metals or redistribute a toxic metal to a more sensitive organ.

The first treatment is always to identify and stop exposure, with urgent supportive and specialist toxicology care.

Iron: essential redox power without a safety valve

Iron overload occurs through inherited increases in absorption (notably HFE-related haemochromatosis), repeated blood transfusion, or acute ingestion — classically a child eating adult iron tablets.

Once transferrin becomes highly saturated, poorly controlled non-transferrin-bound iron enters liver, heart and endocrine cells. Inside cells, ferrous iron can drive the Fenton reaction:

Fe²⁺ + H₂O₂ → Fe³⁺ + OH⁻ + •OH

The hydroxyl radical (•OH) attacks lipids, proteins and DNA almost where it is formed. Chronic injury produces hepatic fibrosis/cirrhosis, diabetes, skin pigmentation, cardiomyopathy, arthropathy and hypogonadism.

Hereditary overload is commonly treated by removing blood (venesection), which forces stored iron into new red cells; transfusion overload requires iron chelators such as deferoxamine or oral agents.

Acute poisoning begins with corrosive gastrointestinal injury and may progress to shock, acidosis and liver failure.

Arsenic: phosphate mimic and thiol poison

Arsenic is a metalloid whose inorganic forms occur naturally in some groundwater, including parts of Nepal's Terai aquifers.

The WHO provisional drinking-water guideline is 10 µg L⁻¹; concentrations above a national operational limit call for an alternative source or effective removal, not reassurance that “a little poison is a nutrient”.

  • Arsenate, As(V), resembles phosphate. It can substitute in phosphorylation reactions, but the arsenate esters hydrolyse readily, wasting metabolic energy (arsenolysis).
  • Arsenite, As(III), binds paired thiol groups, notably lipoamide in pyruvate dehydrogenase and α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Blocking these gateways restricts aerobic ATP production.

Acute poisoning causes severe vomiting, abdominal pain, watery diarrhoea and shock.

Chronic exposure is associated with mottled pigmentation and thickened palms/soles (hyperkeratosis), peripheral neuropathy, vascular disease and cancers of skin, bladder and lung.

Dimercaprol (BAL) was historically designed around arsenic's thiol chemistry; water-soluble chelators such as succimer (DMSA) or DMPS may be used in selected cases.

Public-health control — testing wells and switching to safe water — prevents far more injury than late chelation.

Mercury: the form picks the target organ

Metallic mercury liquid is poorly absorbed from a healthy gut, but its invisible vapour is readily inhaled, crosses the blood–brain barrier and is oxidized and trapped in the nervous system.

Chronic vapour poisoning classically gives tremor, gum and kidney problems and erethism — irritability, shyness and emotional instability. Inorganic mercury salts such as HgCl₂ are corrosive and especially injure gut and kidney.

Microorganisms in aquatic sediments convert inorganic mercury to methylmercury, which binds protein thiols, enters food chains and biomagnifies in predatory fish.

A methylmercury– cysteine complex resembles methionine closely enough to be carried across the blood–brain and placental barriers.

The Minamata disaster in Japan showed the result: numbness, unsteady gait, constricted visual fields, speech and hearing disturbance, and devastating fetal brain injury. “Mercury poisoning” is therefore incomplete as an examination phrase unless the chemical form is specified.

Lead: a calcium/zinc impostor with no safe childhood threshold

Pb²⁺ exploits pathways meant for Ca²⁺, Fe²⁺ and Zn²⁺ and binds thiol and other ligand groups in proteins.

It inhibits δ-aminolaevulinic acid dehydratase and ferrochelatase in haem synthesis, contributing to anaemia and basophilic stippling of red cells. More importantly, lead disturbs neuronal development, synaptic signalling and behaviour.

No safe blood-lead concentration has been identified for children; a reference value is a screening statistic, not a biological safety line.

Sources include deteriorating lead paint, battery recycling, contaminated dust and soil, some traditional remedies/cosmetics, industrial emissions and plumbing components.

Gastrointestinal absorption is greater in children and increases when iron or calcium nutrition is poor. Lead is stored for years in bone and can be released during pregnancy, lactation or bone loss.

Clinical hooks include developmental delay, abdominal colic, constipation, kidney injury, hypertension, peripheral neuropathy such as wrist drop and, at very high exposure, encephalopathy.

Severe cases may receive CaNa₂EDTA, succimer or dimercaprol combinations under specialist direction; removing the source is indispensable because chelation cannot undo established neurodevelopmental injury.

Cadmium: the kidney's long memory

Cadmium enters through tobacco smoke, contaminated rice and other foods, phosphate-fertilizer impurities, nickel–cadmium batteries, pigments and metal work. In blood and liver it induces and binds metallothionein.

The small Cd–metallothionein complex is filtered by the kidney and taken up by proximal tubules, where cadmium accumulates with a biological half-life measured in decades.

Tubular injury leaks low-molecular-mass proteins and wastes phosphate and calcium.

Bone then demineralizes, producing osteomalacia/osteoporosis; severe environmental poisoning in Japan was named Itai-itai (“ouch-ouch”) disease because of intense bone pain and fractures.

Inhaled cadmium compounds are also lung carcinogens.

Unlike acute lead or arsenic poisoning, routine chelation is generally not the answer for chronic cadmium burden because mobilized cadmium may increase renal exposure; prevention and exposure removal dominate management.

One line per poison

Iron rusts from within; arsenic blocks thiol gates; mercury's form chooses the organ; lead imitates calcium and steals development; cadmium settles in the kidney and empties bone.

Common mistake

Five swaps the paper sets: Na⁺ is the extracellular cation and K⁺ the intracellular one — the pump maintains, never reverses, that order; the Na⁺/K⁺ pump is primary active (spends ATP) while SGLT is secondary active (spends the gradient); haem iron is Fe(II) for oxygen binding, transport iron Fe(III) on transferrin; Cr(III) is the essential glucose factor while Cr(VI) is toxic — oxidation state is destiny; and chelation matches the metal: EDTA for lead, BAL or penicillamine for arsenic and mercury, never interchangeably.

Stoichiometry and ATP budget of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump

Problem. A resting neuron hydrolyses 2.0 \times 10^6 ATP molecules via its plasma-membrane \text{Na}^+/\text{K}^+ pump. How many \text{Na}^+ ions are extruded, how many \text{K}^+ ions are imported, and what is the net charge moved out of the cell?

Solution. Each ATP exports 3\text{ Na}^+ and imports 2\text{ K}^+, moving +1 net elementary charge outward.

Thus 6.0 \times 10^6\text{ Na}^+ leave, 4.0 \times 10^6\text{ K}^+ enter, and +2.0 \times 10^6\,e of net positive charge is pumped out (making the interior negative).

Chapter summary

  • Macro- and microminerals differ in required amount, not in importance; chemical form and dose decide benefit or harm.
  • Na⁺ dominates extracellular fluid, K⁺ dominates cytosol, Mg²⁺ partners ATP and chlorophyll, and Ca²⁺ combines a structural role in bone with rapid signalling roles.
  • Zn²⁺ is a redox-inert catalytic/structural ion; Fe and Cu handle oxygen and electrons but must be protein-bound; cobalt reaches human metabolism through microbially made vitamin B₁₂.
  • Nickel has established roles in plants and microbes, while chromium(III)'s supposed essential role in humans remains unproved; chromium(VI) is an important carcinogen.
  • Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is the primary-active 3-out/2-in pump. SGLTs spend the Na⁺ gradient, not ATP directly, to import glucose.
  • Oral rehydration works because intestinal SGLT1 links glucose uptake to Na⁺ and water absorption.
  • Iron overload produces hydroxyl radicals; arsenic blocks thiol enzymes and imitates phosphate; organic mercury biomagnifies and crosses into brain and fetus.
  • Lead injures the developing nervous system without an identified safe childhood threshold, while cadmium accumulates in kidney and secondarily destroys bone.

Answers and explanations — Set A

1. (d) — macrominerals are required in hundreds of milligrams or more per day; the term describes amount, not importance.

2. (a) — Na⁺ is the main extracellular cation and determinant of extracellular osmolality.

3. (c) — K⁺ is concentrated inside cells by Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and membrane selectivity.

4. (b) — Mg²⁺ shields ATP's negative phosphates and is part of the true substrate for many ATP-using enzymes.

5. (a) — Zn²⁺ polarizes bound water in carbonic anhydrase, accelerating CO₂ hydration.

6. (d) — ceruloplasmin carries most plasma copper and oxidizes Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ for transferrin loading.

7. (b) — cobalt sits at the centre of cobalamin's corrin ring.

8. (c) — urease is the classic nickel enzyme of plants and microbes.

9. (b) — each haem binds one Fe²⁺, which reversibly binds O₂ in haemoglobin.

10. (a) — hydroxyapatite is a calcium phosphate crystal, Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂.

11. (d) — Mg²⁺ is held by the chlorin ring of chlorophyll.

12. (c) — memorize 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in, 1 ATP.

13. (a) — ouabain and cardiac glycosides bind and inhibit the pump from outside the cell.

14. (c) — SGLT1 is a 2 Na⁺:1 glucose symporter, suited to extracting the last glucose from the gut.

15. (b) — high-capacity SGLT2 in S1/S2 reabsorbs most filtered glucose; SGLT1 then captures the remainder.

16. (d) — glucose-driven Na⁺ uptake through SGLT1 is followed by water absorption.

17. (c) — As(III) has high affinity for sulfur ligands, particularly paired thiols in lipoamide enzymes.

18. (b) — arsenate resembles phosphate but forms easily hydrolysed esters, wasting energy.

19. (a) — methylmercury biomagnified through fish and shellfish in Minamata Bay.

20. (d) — inhibition at two haem-pathway steps helps produce anaemia and raised precursor levels.

21. (b) — cadmium first accumulates in kidney; tubular mineral wasting and bone demineralization follow.

22. (d) — Cr(VI) as chromate/dichromate is the carcinogenic, strongly oxidizing form; Cr(III) is far less mobile.

Model answer D1: essential elements and their biological roles (10 marks)

Introduction. Bio-inorganic chemistry studies the role of metal ions and inorganic compounds in living systems. About 25 elements are essential.

Bulk elements (C, H, O, N, Na, K, Ca, Mg, P, S, Cl) are needed in large amounts and trace elements (Fe, Zn, Cu, Mn, Co, Mo, I, Se) in very small amounts.

Roles of the main metal ions.

  1. Sodium and potassium. Na⁺ is the main extracellular cation, and K⁺ is the main intracellular cation. Together they set osmotic balance, nerve impulses and muscle contraction. The sodium-potassium pump (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase) uses one ATP to push 3\ \text{Na}^+ out and 2\ \text{K}^+ in against their concentration gradients, which makes the cell interior negative.
  2. Magnesium. The central atom of chlorophyll (a porphyrin-type chlorin ring), it is also a cofactor of ATP-using enzymes.
  3. Calcium. The main component of bones and teeth (hydroxyapatite, Ca₁₀(PO₄)₆(OH)₂), and it is needed for blood clotting, muscle contraction and nerve signals.
  4. Iron. The central metal of haemoglobin and myoglobin (oxygen transport and storage), cytochromes (electron transfer) and ferredoxins.
  5. Zinc. Present in over 300 enzymes, such as carbonic anhydrase (which converts CO₂ and water to carbonic acid) and carboxypeptidase.
  6. Copper. Found in cytochrome oxidase, plastocyanin and in haemocyanin, the blue oxygen carrier of molluscs.
  7. Cobalt. The central metal of vitamin B₁₂ (cyanocobalamin), needed for red-blood-cell formation.
  8. Molybdenum and iodine. Mo is in nitrogenase, which fixes atmospheric nitrogen, and I is in thyroxine, so deficiency causes goitre.
Element Compound or site Deficiency disease
Fe haemoglobin anaemia
Ca bone rickets, osteoporosis
I thyroxine goitre
Zn enzymes poor growth, slow healing
Co vitamin B₁₂ pernicious anaemia
Na/K pump cramps, weakness

Oxygen transport. In haemoglobin the Fe²⁺ sits in the haem group. It binds O₂ reversibly, and the four subunits show cooperativity. CO binds about 200 times more strongly than O₂, which makes it poisonous.

In Nepal, iodised salt programmes have greatly reduced goitre in the hill districts.

Numerical. Haemoglobin contains 0.34\% iron by mass and each molecule has four Fe atoms, so the molar mass is \dfrac{4\times55.85}{0.0034} = 6.6\times10^4\ \text{g mol}^{-1}. One gram of haemoglobin binds \dfrac{4\times22.4}{65\,700} = 1.4\ \text{mL} of O₂ at STP.

Conclusion. Metal ions are central to oxygen transport, photosynthesis, nerve action and enzymes, and both deficiency and excess cause disease.

Model answer D2: toxic metals, chelation and metal-based drugs (10 marks)

Introduction. A metal that is useful at a low level may be poisonous at a high level, and heavy metals such as Pb, Hg, Cd and As are toxic even in traces because they bind strongly to sulphur and nitrogen donor groups of enzymes and block them.

Toxic metals.

Metal Source Effect
Lead old paints, petrol, pipes damages the brain and the blood-forming system, reduces intelligence in children
Mercury fish (methylmercury), thermometers, amalgam nerve damage, Minamata disease
Cadmium batteries, plating kidney damage, itai-itai disease
Arsenic groundwater skin lesions, cancer (a problem in the Terai of Nepal)
Chromium(VI) tanning, plating carcinogenic

Chelation therapy. A chelating agent binds a metal ion through two or more donor atoms, giving a stable, soluble, excretable ring complex.

  1. EDTA (as Ca-EDTA) for lead poisoning.
  2. BAL (British anti-Lewisite, 2,3-dimercaptopropanol) for arsenic, mercury and gold.
  3. Desferrioxamine for iron overload and D-penicillamine for copper (Wilson's disease).
  4. Prussian blue for thallium and caesium.

Metal-based drugs.

  • Cisplatin, cis-[\text{Pt(NH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2], an anticancer drug that binds to the guanine bases of DNA. The trans isomer is inactive.
  • Auranofin (gold) for rheumatoid arthritis.
  • Barium sulphate as a contrast agent for X-rays (insoluble, so safe).
  • Lithium carbonate for bipolar disorder.
  • Zinc and iron supplements for deficiency.

Environmental points. The WHO limit for arsenic in drinking water is 10\ \text{ppb} (Nepal's interim standard is 50\ \text{ppb}), the limit for lead is 10\ \text{ppb}, and methods of removal include sand filtration with iron oxide and the SORAS technique (solar oxidation and removal of arsenic).

Numerical. A 0.5\ \text{L} sample of water has 25\ \mu\text{g} of arsenic, which is \dfrac{25}{0.5} = 50\ \mu\text{g L}^{-1} = 50\ \text{ppb}, five times the WHO limit of 10\ \text{ppb}. A person drinking 3\ \text{L} per day takes in 150\ \mu\text{g} of arsenic.

Conclusion. Heavy metals poison enzymes, chelating agents remove them, and complexes such as cisplatin turn the same binding power into medicine.
